No. I rebounded hard—straight into the open, masochistic arms of Dota 2.

And let me tell you: it was like crawling out of a frat house fight pit and stumbling into a sadistic chess tournament being played by Russian AIs with gambling addictions. This isn’t a game. There’s no “meta”—there’s only pain, and ten dudes yelling in five languages about “item timings” while your tower disintegrates like your self-esteem.

Dota 2 is the game you play when you’ve hit rock bottom in League and decided to dig deeper. It doesn’t hold your hand. At first, I honestly thought Delta Force was way more creative and enjoyable than the mess that is BF2042. But after grinding over 336 hours and seeing the game crawl its way to the so-called S4 stage, I can tell you—the whole thing is falling apart fast.

Cheaters everywhere, zero action from devs:
Every single match you see players snapping onto targets at inhuman speed. Feels like half the lobby is running aimbot and nobody's doing a damn thing about it. It completely ruins the experience, and it’s obvious the devs either don’t care or are totally incompetent.

Final thoughts:

It’s hard to overstate how magical [i]Stardew Valley[/i] really is. It starts as a simple farming game, but quickly blossoms into one of the most emotionally rich, comforting, and addictively satisfying games ever made. Whether you’re fishing at 8 a.m. in a pixelated fog, giving someone their favorite birthday gift, or just planting beans while rain taps gently in the background, [i]Stardew [/i]has this almost sacred ability to slow time down and remind you that life can be soft, quiet, and meaningful.

It’s not just a farming sim. It’s a place you live in. A place you return to when you’re tired, overwhelmed, or just need a little joy. And it was made by one person. That still blows my mind.

🌱 [b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] A slow, beautiful life on your terms. Whether you want to farm, fish, mine, romance, decorate, or just walk around petting your animals, [i]Stardew [/i]lets you play at your own pace. There’s no pressure. You can optimize for gold and rare crops, or you can just vibe and grow turnips while chatting with Shane about how bad life used to be. It’s your little world.

[*] One of the best farming loops ever created. There’s something endlessly satisfying about planting seeds, watering them, harvesting them, then reinvesting in even more complex crops or artisan goods. The loop is tight, clean, and deeply rewarding. It scratches that perfect simulation itch.

[*] A cast of characters that feel real. The people of Pelican Town aren’t perfect. Some are prickly, some are shy, some are struggling. And over time, you see them change. You hear their pasts, uncover their trauma, celebrate their birthdays, and maybe even fall in love. Even characters I disliked at first grew on me, because they’re written like real people, not just game mechanics.

[*] Gorgeous pixel art and serene music. The visuals are simple, but warm and expressive. Every season has its own palette and charm. And the soundtrack? It’s iconic. Peaceful, nostalgic, and instantly grounding. Every track feels like a warm mug of something sweet.

[*] The best version of “daily tasks” you’ll ever find. Watering plants, checking the coop, upgrading tools, remembering villagers’ schedules—it sounds like work, but it feels like love. The rhythm of a [i]Stardew [/i]day is cozy, not stressful. You do what you can. You go to bed when you're ready. It’s a reminder that routine can be a gift, not a grind.

[*] Freedom to play however you want. There’s no "wrong" way to play. Want to marry Emily and become a wine magnate? Go for it. Want to live alone, max out the Community Center, and raise cows? You’re valid. Want to spend five in-game years just fishing and watching the leaves fall? That’s living, baby.

[*] Mines, combat, and mysteries. Beyond the surface-level farming sim is a full-on dungeon crawler with weapons, gear upgrades, and secrets to uncover. 

[*] Incredible post-launch support. ConcernedApe has continued to update the game for free for years. New festivals, dialogue, late-game systems, and even co-op? He didn’t have to do that, but he did, and it shows how much love is poured into this game.

[*] It’s multiplayer now—and still feels magical. Whether you're building a farm with your partner, tending animals with friends, or just running around gifting villagers together, multiplayer doesn’t break the game’s peaceful energy. It amplifies it.

[*] It stays with you. Long after you put it down, you’ll remember your favorite spouse, your cat’s name, the layout of your first farm, or that one perfect autumn day when you found a prismatic shard and felt like a god.
[/list]

💔 [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Lol. Imagine thinking [i]Stardew Valley[/i] has cons. (Okay fine: some people don’t like real-time energy systems or pixel graphics, and that’s valid—but it’s not the game's fault fault you don’t like comfort.)
[/list]

[h1]Proud Revenue, Worrying Future: Short-Term Profit at the Cost of Ruined Reputation [/h1]

[h2]5.5/10 [/h2]

[h3]Opening [/h3]

Shadowverse has always been unique among CCG. This work, released in 2016, has gained a group of loyal and considerable players with its Japanese anime art, funny evolution system, and decent rewards. However, due to worrying revenue and concessions to the Shadowverse: World Beyond project, it has stopped updating in the past year. Both Cygames and many fans have high expectations for this sequel - however, the greater the expectation, the greater the disappointment.

After waves of publicity, Shadowverse: World Beyond was officially announced yesterday(June 17, 2025). This work demonstrates improvements in graphics and gameplay and introduces a large-scale multiplayer social sandbox - Shadowverse Park, which is rare in card games. It can be called a next-generation CCG without a doubt. The game's commercial performance is also outstanding. Not only did it top the Google Play free game lists, earning approximately 380 million yen(approximately 2.62 million USD) in revenue, it also topped the Steam #1 top seller, with a peak online user of 110,000. However, compared to its predecessor, Shadowverse: World Beyond has an overwhelmingly bad reputation among players. The reason is that the game has a toxic economic design, the blatant greed and money-hungry shown by the developer have become the key to pushing the game at the center of controversy.

[h3]Strength [/h3]

Like Hearthstone, Magic: The Gathering, Shadowverse: World Beyond uses a battlefield interaction design based on creatures. Although the deck has up to 40 cards, both sides have only 20 health, the overall rhythm of the round is pretty fast. The game does not have class-specific skills, yet chooses to provide a diverse experience through exclusive cards with different class characteristics and effects. The game also introduces a powerful super evolution mechanism this time, adding new possibilities to the tactics. The art and music also continue the excellent level of the previous work.

Shadowverse: World Beyond's tutorial could be seen as well-detailed, and the PVE content is comparatively rich. The single-player story features full voice acting and incorporates Live 2D performance. Though the narrative might be somewhat fragmented and clichéd, the reading experience as a visual novel is quite outstanding. Shadowverse: World Beyond also introduces a guaranteed mechanism for getting the highest rarity legendary card in 10 packs, which is recalculated upon appearance. I can say frankly that this is the easiest CCG I have ever played to get high-rarity cards. There are daily free packs that are excluded from the guaranteed, and players will not lose points or drop ranks below the master. The rank scores here are calculated entirely based on in-game performance, and grouping has replaced the rank as the standard for measuring skills. Such mechanisms and features are the highlights of Shadowverse: World Beyond. But yeah, at what cost?

[h3]Weakness [/h3]

The cost of Shadowverse: World Beyond packs has increased nearly five times compared to the previous work, but the efficiency of obtaining rupees has merely gone up twice. Even with sufficient Day 1 rewards and a high drop rate for Legendary cards, most players still can't build one fully capable deck, and the current reward for the single-player mode is only about ten packs. In addition to resource inflation, this work also forces you only to liquefy more than 3 surplus cards. Numerous cards are completely unusable, and many players specialize in a single or several classes. However, disenchant, which people assume is normal in other CCGs, becomes rather difficult in Shadowverse: World Beyond. The risk of card creation grows worse. Not to mention that Shadowverse: World Beyond will bring a new expansion pack in the next one or two months, the latest powerful cards will require players to spend a lot of resources to obtain, and at least for now, the acquisition of resources within the game is exceedingly scarce.

The significant difference in effects and values between Legendary and regular cards became the last straw that led to overwhelmingly negative reviews for Shadowverse: World Beyond. I have tried many CCGs myself and I can say that the current environment is incredibly toxic, one can even be viewed as a P2W game for now. The restrictions on card decomposition make it almost impossible for players to create enough Legendary, even Gold cards for a deck, and you can include a maximum of 3 same cards. While most players may only have 1-3 Legendary in their decks and can only hope for luck, many heavy spenders already have 8 or more, making it easier to draw, then crush, and reverse the situation. The overall matching system is quite unbalanced, cross-rank and cross-group matching is not rare, the server performance is quite bad too. Fortunately, they only affect the menu and other interactions and do not affect the round. The leader skins are included in the pack, the probability is only 0.06%, and they have been separated into three parts. It takes nearly 650 draws to obtain them completely; even the most toxic and widely criticized miHoYo-like pool among gacha pales in comparison.

[h3]Conclusion [/h3]

I could understand that the fundamental goal of commercial games is essentially to make a profit, but this doesn't justify developers exploiting players to the fullest extent possible. Shadowverse: World Beyond's current business mode is so toxic that it is something unprecedented even by the standards of card games and gacha. Cygames did not figure out the advantages of its predecessor and its basic player base; with the game's art no longer has an advantage in today's increasingly saturated card game market, and the decent rewards that once shone are gone here. With the Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel has a deeper card pool, and though its environment is extreme, the rewards are somewhat gorgeous, even though many F2P players can easily put together one powerful deck. Undeniably, old competitors such as Hearthstone and Magic: The Gathering have improved their rewards in recent years. Shadowverse: World Beyond's move may generate revenue in the short term, but it is cutting off its arms and completely consuming its original advantages.

Anyway, Shadowverse: World Beyond has indeed made some improvements in graphics, gameplay, and plot performance, and the Shadowverse park and rich PVE content could add a certain amount of fun. But as a competitive card game with PVP as its core, if the balance hasn't been reached, no matter how many other features are included, it will be meaningless. I am worried about its future, in the first expansion pack it has already shown such obvious P2W tendencies and huge balance issues, and I can't imagine what's next; Even so, it cannot be said that this game is worthless. The early version of any card game has a very shallow pool, which is the best time to get into; since Weiß Schwarz has no plans to launch a video game, Shadoweverse: World Beyonds can still maintain its dominant position in the anime CCG. But this does not mean that Cygames can sit back and relax. The current outstanding profit comes at the cost of a bad reputation, old players do not receive much compensation, and the player retention rate is worrying in the long run as well. Shadowverse: World Beyond is completely depleting the long-term value of the entire game - and perhaps even the future of the IP itself, I sincerely wish Cygames could take action as soon as possible and not lose the opportunity in stillness, and completely ruin the trust of the player, and the future of this work full of potential.

[b] TLDR: 2000+ hour veteran who fell in love with a tactical masterpiece in 2017, now watches it die a slow death because of the soul-crushing changes that Ubisoft has, and continues to implement to this game [/b]

[h1] The Rise and Fall of Rainbow Six Siege [/h1]

I first played R6 in 2017 on my PS4. It was my first realistic tactical FPS and I was completely hooked by the unique gameplay loop and mechanics. I was lowkey addicted, platinumed the game in 2 years, grinding ranked with friends from 7  AM to 5 PM during high school summers, and continued playing when I got my PC setup. I witnessed what was in my opinion the rise (2016-2021), downfall, and funeral of the R6 I knew and loved playing.

[h2] When Everything Started Going Wrong [/h2]

The beginning of the end was when the Ubisoft split the R6 devs to create this new game called R6 Extraction. To give some context, there was a limited time mode called Outbreak during operation Chimera where it was like R6 and COD Zombies had a baby. It was pretty fun while it lasted and it was well received by the community, but poopisoft decided to make it a separate paid game that expanded on it. Content creators given early access to that game had some pretty negative things to say about the game and same thing goes for when it was released for the public. While all this was happening, R6 started losing its soul and gained so much downhill momentum that even the original developers couldn't recover the losses. The quality and quantity of the content dropped significantly and below are some examples:
[list]
    [*] [b] One operator per season [/b] with recycled guns (we used to get two operators with new weapons and a new, not reworked, map)
    [*] [b] New gun/s every 2-3 seasons [/b] instead of with every operator release
    [*] [b] Map reworks nobody asked for [/b] that the commmunity either hates or bans constantly in ranked
    [*] [b] The original recruit removed [/b], one of the last pieces of original content that made the game fun 
[/list]
The list goes on but this review is already going to be very long.

[h2] What Made Siege Special is Gone [/h2]

The developers listened too much to crying pros instead of preserving what made the game fun. The game took a turn and started sacrificing realism and tacticalness for balancing sake:
[list]
    [*] [b] Caveira's old pistol [/b]- reworked, not as fun anymore
    [*] [b] Ash and Jager ACOGs [/b]- removed (R4-C acog is back but it was gone for a very long time and it is not the same as it was before)
    [*] [b] 2-second timer before detection when going outside as a defender [/b]- removed, apparently attackers know the exact and precise location of your character's head the moment your toe touches the outside of a building
    [*] [b] Widespread ACOG availability [/b]- stripped away and replaced with 1.5x scopes that in my opinion, didn't change much and did not address the root of the problem they were trying to solve and arguably made it worse
    [*] [b] Valkyrie cams being placeable outside [/b]- removed
    [*] [b] Zofia's withstand ability [/b]- banished (okay so this one was actually unfair and turned the tides on one pro-league round, but it was moving toward an interesting idea of operator-specific passives unique to their lore that I would have liked)
[/list]

[h3] The Fortnite-ification of Siege [/h3]

The game gave off mobile game and fortnite vibes with how beginner friendly and arcadey it felt after some changes. No shade to mobile games and fortnite as I enjoy them too, but what makes them enjoyable is not something that R6 should also implement, but unfortunately did which ruined the immersion and realism:
[list]
    [*] [b] Mobile game-like UI [/b] that destroyed immersion and I aesthetically didn't like
    [*] [b] Enemy outlines [/b] where there used to be none
    [*] [b] Free base game operators [/b] (you used to have to earn them)
    [*] [b] Free attachments [/b] (another thing you had to work for)
    [*] [b] Battle passes [/b] locking cosmetics behind a paywall for a game I already bought. Free games like fortnite or apex legends make most of their money through cosmetics but for a paid game like R6, just put new free content in the bag bro
    [*] [b] Ridiculous skins [/b] that shatter any sense of tactical realism. Don't get me wrong I love the april fools cosmetics but it has gone out of hand with the new paragon skins that look like they came straight out of valorant.
[/list]

[h3] What I Miss Most [/h3]
  
[list]
    [*] [b] Night maps and old graphics [/b] that felt atmospheric
    [*] [b] Plane map and other classics [/b] are unplayable. The Plane map is not even in the casual map-pool and only in custom game. The new House and Hereford Base map is too different from the old map to call it a rework.
    [*] [b] Situations mode and Original Terrorist Hunt [/b]- situations were a nice and challenging way to learn the ropes of the game and introduces the player to the lore of the game. It also used to be a way to play old maps that were reworked.
    [*] [b] Recruit Rushing [/b] 
    [*] [b] The lighting, old recoil, and slow-paced tactical gameplay [/b] (could be a skill issue because everyone sucked back then and didnt treat this game like COD search and destroy)
    [*] [b] Realistic Operator trailers [/b] when you first unlock them
[/list]

[h2] Sound is Horrendous [/h2]

For a tactical shooter that makes you heavily rely on sound to locate enemies, it is pretty unreliable and makes you question whether you suck, need a new headset, or the sound design sucks (its this one btw). Im pretty sure my hair loss is due to me pulling my hair everytime I die to an enemy which sounded like they were coming from the opposite direction.

[h2] Cheating Epidemic [/h2]

From 2021 to 2024 was when I started mainly playing on PC and cheating was absolutely rampant. While it's somewhat under control now (Im not entirely sure as I dont play much ranked nowadays but I hear its gotten better), it felt like poopisoft was prioritizing other stuff instead of their anti-cheat. Don't even get me started on xim and MnK users in console controller only lobbies.

[h1] The Final Nail: Operation Siege X [/h1]

They hyped this as "a new era of siege" that they'd have been working on for years, the "biggest transformation" claiming to make siege great again by improving graphics, developing core elements resulting in more tactical gameplay, and new ways to play. I still had hope. I installed the game and the new update, and played a few games. Didn't notice any huge difference on both graphics and gameplay. New ways to play? meta was still the same with same objectives and standard approach to each objective from both sides. Felt stale and bland. I immediately realized this IS what siege is now, it is definitely not for veterans who remember what made this game special. Since they advertised this as the "new era of siege", I slowly came to the realization that the siege I fell in love with a long time ago is dead and will never come back and this new siege is what the developers intend to expand on in the coming of years. 

I immediately uninstalled. It just wasn't fun anymore.

[h2] For New Players [/h2]

If you're looking for a tactical, realistic FPS experience, you're about 7 years too late. The closest I've gotten to that original R6 adrenaline rush was from playing Escape from Tarkov and Arena Breakout: Infinite.

[h3] The Verdict [/h3]

Rainbow Six Siege 2016-2020 was a tactical masterpiece. Rainbow Six Siege 2025 is a hollow, arcadey, and cash-grabbing shell giving you the bare minimum while wearing the corpse of that masterpiece as a skin.

The game I loved is dead. This review is its eulogy.

I thought the game would end. That I would uninstall it. That I’d move on.

That was before the leather.

RimWorld taught me things no other game dared whisper. It stripped away the facade. It showed me that survival isn’t noble. It’s just a series of ugly calculations. A pile of flesh balanced against a ticking hunger bar. There is no morality—only math.

It started in the game. Always in the game.

The first time I harvested a raider, it was necessity. No cloth. No muffalo. No trade ships. Just bodies—so many bodies. My colonists were cold. One shivered in bed, near death from hypothermia. The game gave me a solution. A menu option.
“Butcher Human (Details).”

I clicked. There was no music. Just the sound of slicing. Then warmth. Then silence. he coats fit perfectly. And suddenly, I saw the beauty in it. A brutal elegance. Every corpse became a resource. Every raid, a gift. I began to plan. I stopped capturing for ransom. I captured for yield. I calculated how many jackets a torso could give me before rot set in. Then I began naming the jackets. Each one carried a story. A life, repurposed. Raiders who screamed, colonists who begged, wanderers who chose the wrong path. They all became part of the colony. Eternal. Useful.

But the game wouldn’t stop. Even when I closed it, I could still hear the meat grinder. The squelch of skin on steel. I’d sit in meetings and wonder how many jackets I could make from everyone in the room. I’d watch the news and think, "That’s 60 kilos of raw material." It wasn’t a thought. It was instinct.

The colony had followed me home. I started building. Small things. Cooling systems. Drains. Bleach stations. Not real yet, just diagrams. But they felt right. Efficient. Optimized. I bought leather-working tools. At first, it was deer hide. Then pigskin. Then something unmarked, from a seller who didn’t ask questions. I practiced. I improved. I stopped shaking when I cut. And now, I wait. For the first opportunity. The first visitor. The first stranger who wanders too close. Because the colony never ended. I’m just playing it on a different map now.

Review: RimWorld — The Infinite Game of Stories

RimWorld isn’t just a game — it’s a story generator that keeps on giving, hour after glorious hour. For the price, it’s an absolute steal. There are few games out there that offer this level of depth, replayability, and sheer emergent madness at such a low cost.

Want a cozy, Stardew Valley-style farming sim with gentle pacing and a soft ambient soundtrack? RimWorld can do that.

Want a brutal, real-time (well, real-pause-time) survival sim with starvation, frostbite, organ harvesting, and the ever-looming threat of mechanoid annihilation? RimWorld’s got you covered.

Want to roleplay as a band of drugged-out, inbred nobles wielding plasma swords and ranting about their lineage while being swarmed by psychotic man-eating rabbits? Come right in, my liege.

With its mod support, layered AI storytelling, and the sheer randomness of each generated world, no two playthroughs are ever the same. You'll laugh. You'll cry. You’ll rage-quit. And five minutes later, you’ll start a new colony, because just maybe this time, Randy Random will go easy on you.

Verdict:
If you like strategy, sims, survival, storytelling, chaos, or just watching a Yorkshire terrier rip apart a raider's throat while your colonist overdoses on flake... RimWorld is for you.

Odyssey was a last straw for me. As many others, I want to like this game, but unlike many others, I can`t convince myself that I do.
Initially Rimworld managed to sell as concept and idea, which are loved by many - a storytelling sandbox colony manager.
But that "storyteller" part is just a lazy excuse for absence of any meaningful balance or in-depth mechanics. 
To be short, your base gameplay always devolves into unending onslaught of infinite enemy hordes with stupid AI, because all major events are raids and stupid random events, such as diseases and random power network explosions. Devs just couldn`t come up with anything better, and their understanding of difficulty is very limited. 
Base game is terrible. And Rimworld is notorious for it`s massive modding community. The only way to play Rimworld without starting to hate everything about it is with mods.
And I say you that - modded gameplay is awesome and sometimes astonishing. Because it delivers on initial concept of a sandbox colony manager and adventurous gameplay, which creates actually interesting situations other than "another suicidal wave of 200 morons killed themselves in our meta killbox which we had to build because game design in this game is sнit". 
As a matter of fact, modders just developed this game instead of devs, because a majority of mods are QoL. And oh boy, you gonna need them. Remember about bad game design? It is everywhere, even in small details.

Every mechanism which houses components will constantly break down, requiring you to waste already limited resources on repairs. It doesn`t add any depth to gameplay, all it adds is a source of tedium and irritation. Clothing and armor deteriorate over time, and there is no option to repair them. Yes, of course i can add mods that remove breakdowns and allow to repair armor or even remove deterioration, but those things had to be thought through by the devs, not fixed by modders. And don`t even start me that it is supposed to be that way, that`s just a very bad design choice. 
And such things are all over the place.

Unfortunately, Ludeon has a habit of taking best and most popular mods out there and, without any credit to modders, they turn them into overpriced DLCs, which, in case of Odyssey, have even less content than original mod, and add even more idiotic mechanics. 
In Odyssey, there is no space combat. You can`t leave the planet on a gravship and start NG+. You can`t attach spaceship parts of original endgame quest to your gravship to finish the game. When you leave a world tile using your gravship, this tile gets destroyed forever, if you haven`t built a special device which prevents the destruction. 
Why in the world such mechanic even exists? I don`t care about lore implications, all I can tell from the design choice itself is that they had coding issues regarding tiles and had to add a crutch, or someone is just stupid.
DLC doesn`t change base gameplay, which, to this day, is riddled with obnoxious issues. It functions as one-time side quest, just as Anomaly did.
Community developed a stockholm syndrom towards devs, because latter have all the rights to use modders work for free without notice, and they even stated that in their EULA, and no one can do anything about it.

But I don`t want to support that or ignore, suppressing my critical thinking. All of the above is a great example of great game concept, ruined by unhealthy and greedy dev practices. When I play this game, I just feel abused.

And I would rather pay modders than devs. They do much more work, and they do it for free.

But what killed me most is that they finally added heavy bridges, but paywalled them behind DLC instead of adding to the base game where they belong. That is just laughable.

Very disappointed with this game from both a visual and gameplay perspective.

Gameplay leaves a lot to be desired here. The building mechanics are incredibly janky, making it sometimes impossible to lay buildings out in any formation that isn't just a standard box.  The game also advertises pal automation of base operations, but this functionality is incredibly limiting. Pals can be set to automatically complete a job for you, and gather resources; however, more advanced multi-step recipes can't be preplanned for automation. This becomes a huge problem in the late game when you need better balls to catch strong pals to level up. Crafting high level balls is an enormous chore, and makes the end game grind unbearable.

Pal customization is also a chore and a bore that doesn't pay off. Since every Pal can learn every move/trait in the game, and Pals not having their own unique base stats, different Pals are effectively just a skin. The only two unique aspects of a Pal are their underwhelming passive abilities and their typing.  The meaning of a Pal's stats is even further diminished by Level heavily influencing Pal damage output. If I create a level 40 Pal with all their stats superior to a level 50 Pal, I will still lose the fight because of level alone.

Speaking of the fights, combat in this game is awful. There is very little agency to battle. Pals use moves on their own, with only some Pals having a special attack you can activate with almost no feedback to the user as to whether you successfully activated the skill or not. The most "strategic" way to play I've seen is being able to recall a Pal before they get hit then resummoning them since there appears to be no cooldown on summoning. You can also run around shooting things yourself, but player damage seems greatly inferior to Pal damage, and isn't particularly engaging on its own either. For a game advertising itself so heavily on its monster taming aspects, I would expect far more engaging combat involving the monsters.

So let me get the part out of the way most people will want to know...is Elden RIng Nightreign as bad as people said on here early on? Absolutely not. Is it a 10/10 like Elden Ring was? Absolutely not. This is a completely different kind of game that needs to be played with a mostly different type of mindset. This is a rogue-like / Souls-like game that expects you to move fast and know what you are doing. You will not be awarded for playing slowly, exploring. However even though this game has tons of flaws (And after like 30 hours of game time) I really ended up enjoying the game. I have faith Fromsoft will fix (Most) of the issues the game suffers from. They already have fixed some by the time I write this. At best I would say the game is a 7/10. Which for me means simply above average. The rogue like elements (currently) hold the game back from being as great as it should be. For now let me go over some of the Positive and Negative things about the game.

Positive
---------
+ Honestly the game is fun with friends and (Sometimes) with randoms. 

+ The different characters and play styles they bring.

+ The remembrance Quests are great and worth doing. (The Que is an issue though)

+ The Nightlord / Original bosses (For the most part) are all honestly great additions! The main issue ends up being how you (Practice) them.

+ Fast paced (40+ minute long) sessions for each expedition. 

+ Honestly some pretty epic moments can happen with a good group that I will remember for a good while!

+ The returning bosses from Dark Souls 1,2 and 3 are a fun experience! Tons from Elden Ring of course but seeing the Souls Bosses makes me happy.

+ Not having to worry about how my character is being built stat wise. Some people may not like this and I understand that however with how this game works...that would not do well. It could take much more time than needed for the fact this is a fast paced game.

+ Unlike Elden Ring this game makes playing around with weapons fun. In Elden Ring it can take forever to get something good. In Elden Ring i have to change my build OVER and OVER. In this though I can actually try out things and I love it. As a Souls one trick Great Sword Pony...it has felt refreshing that I could try other things / builds without having to respec a thousand times. Makes me wanna try out some stuff in Elden Ring now.

Negative
-----------
- While playing with friends is amazing and sometimes randoms can be also...more than likely if you play without friends and 2 randoms you will end up with an absolutely terrible group that can make progress close to impossible unless you yourself end up carrying. Which is not always fun.

- 40+ minute long expeditions are fine. However Nightreign has had some pretty bad server issues here and there. If your session gets screwed over you will get nothing at all. You will only have wasted 40 minutes of your life because of something out of your control. Sometimes you may D/C and be able to rejoin but sometimes the game won't let you...and then threatens to penalize you. Which is absurd.

- No Duo is a huge let down for me. Of course Fromsoft plans on adding it but i'm gonna be real. There was no excuse to ship the game without Duo's. Delaying the game would have been the best option. Sometimes you and a friend can do great even if a third player leaves or hold you back but like...being punished by a boss being scaled for three players is still annoying.

- Needs more classes honestly. I love what they have going with them (even if some feel much better than others)

- The 40+ minute run back. You know in Dark Souls / Elden Ring when you die? You remember the corpse run you do getting back to the boss? Those usually were pretty quick...however this game gives you no way of practicing the new bosses in general. You will eventually get used to them but until then enjoy dying learning the boss pattern. Even in solo where things are now easier you will still be punished if you did not (Get good) enough on your first run. It just takes away the fun for a good while.

- Bosses are weak against certain elements however you are not guaranteed a elemental area with a weapon for your class. Which kinda blows. Sure you can use the gems to bring one in yourself but that's not the point.

- The Gems / Relics etc. The randomness factor (Rogue like Game) is...honestly kinda depressing. It's harder to get a good gem in this than it is in Diablo 4. To be fair the recent patch did add an end game vendor that is great but before that it's beyond random. You don't get to take much with you into a run. I wish the game handled each runs start like Dead Cells honestly.

- I do wish there were more returning Souls 1,2 and 3 bosses. 

- The remembrance Que issue and getting into a match sometimes. When this is fixed I will remove this.

- No voice chat or even Chat in general. Would love a RETREAT option or something...Since randoms have issues understanding what is going on sometimes with just a simple ping.

Like what your ACTUAL abilities ACTUALLY and FULLY do. The weapon scaling stuff + character scaling stuff. Just so much information is only in here and people now of days have a case of the zoomies...speaking of.

- The fact this game is all about the zoomies. I get it. It's not Elden Ring. But still not being able to really explore kinda blows. The Battle Royal death storm / circle I feel still happens too fast / moves faster than needed. I am not saying take it out. Just calibrate it a little more. Heck you can survive in the storm for awhile before it just instantly kills you...which also sucks.

Because when you pick your souls back up you get them back + (Most I think) of your souls from the level loss back as well. Why? Just get rid of the level loss in general. Welcome to Nightreign, the small multiplayer version of Elden Ring. It's not a sequel, not "Elden Ring 2." It's a different game. And anyone who doesn't understand that before clicking "New Game" has already lost and is clearly in the wrong place.

Anyone hoping for an open world, for the majestic elegance of FromSoft's world design, for an adventure that slowly swallows you up with epic grandeur—they'll be crushed by the game's blunt edge. In Nightreign, you die often. Very often. And usually in ways that make you doubt your experience as a player. But if you love rogue-lites—games like Hades -then you'll suddenly realize: There's something there. Something unique. Something hard, cold, honest. Every meter counts, every return journey after death is a silent meditation on mistakes. Accordingly, this game functions as a rogue-lite with Souls DNA. The world is fragmented, changing with each playthrough, losing and gaining structure. You die, you lose. Again and again. But not everything is gone: knowledge, certain progress, some currencies remain – enough to motivate you. Not enough to give you hope.

But that's precisely its appeal: anyone who sees the game as Elden Ring will hate it. However, anyone who realizes it's a rogue-lite with a Soulslike flair will suddenly understand what Nightreign really is. It's a game for people who can lose and still keep going. For people who see progress in every death. A learning experience, or at least a sad little "aha." It's aimed at a very specific target audience. People who could never get enough of Hades. Players who got a little angrier with every death in Legacy, but also a little better. And those who play Souls games not simply for the big world and the lore, but because they love the pain. The challenge. The compulsion to improve themselves.

It's fantastic and it's fun if you really get into it. Have fun. ;D

Nightreign's announcement initially sparked some controversy due to its dramatic departure from the traditional Souls gameplay. As someone who spent a lot of time undecided on whether to try it out, I decided to give it a chance, and I'm glad I did, despite its notable shortcomings.

The core gameplay experience is fundamentally different from previous FromSoftware titles, which definitely won't appeal to every Souls veteran. While most might be used to the patient, methodical style of gameplay in previous titles, this won’t help you too much in Nightreign. Instead, this game operates on a strict two day timer where you must prepare to face one of eight Nightlords as one of 8 pre-made characters, each with their own sets of skills, stat structures and proficiencies.

The gameplay in Nightreign borrows heavily from battle royale mechanics, in which you're dropped into a map that gradually shrinks in explorable areas over the course of each in game day, encouraging strategic route planning. Each morning the map resets, but as night falls, you're corralled into a small area for a scripted boss encounter. Reading the map becomes an essential skill; every location offers tempting rewards like elemental weapons suited to defeat your chosen Nightlord, healing flask charges or talismans. Despite this, simply going after treasure isn’t enough, you really need to balance it out by hunting down bosses littered across the map in order to ensure that you’re leveling up enough in the mean time, creating a tense risk-reward dynamic that might clash with Souls veterans taking a more patient and methodical approach.

The eight available characters each offer distinct specializations, strengths, and weaknesses. Major abilities on cooldown timers really differentiate them: the Wylder can grapple bosses or pull enemies closer for example, the Revenant can summon creatures and specializes in faith based magic, and the Recluse can generate infinite FP for spellcasting. Learning these character specific skills is crucial for success.

The progression system includes Murk, a persistent currency earned across matches that's used to purchase cosmetic skins and relics. These relics function similarly to Bloodborne's runes, providing significant bonuses that can dramatically enhance specific character aspects, whether its flat stat increases, or even improving a selected characters skill, sometimes quite dramatically.

While the map includes interesting modifiers such as snowy mountains, elevated Nox ruins, underground flaming temples amidst pools of magma, and scarlet rot-infested forests, it begins to feel a little stale after extended play. I’d definitely like to see one or two added maps eventually, each with their own modifiers.

More frustrating is the missed opportunity with existing FromSoftware content. While some other players have called out From’s blatant reuse of existing assets, one of my more glaring complaints is that they didn’t reuse enough! Since it’s all in the same engine, I feel as though they could have easily lifted and shifted more content from older games, particularly from titles older than Elden Ring. There’s an insane amount of content they could have borrowed from, and considering this title’s clear rogue-like approach, there actually isn’t really that much content all things considered. I actually felt like the weapons were quite limited per category, and some of the bonuses and perks you collect from defeating bosses were quite uninteresting and lackluster, though I do understand that this is a From game, so including ridiculously overpowered abilities isn’t really uniform to the series.

Aside being fairly light on content, Nightreign's multiplayer design has some glaring issues. The game supports three players or solo play, yet there is no duo option, which doesn’t make a lot of sense considering a player can leave and the game scales down to the two remaining players. If the scaling is already there, why on earth isn’t it an option in the first place?! I also found it bizarre that the roundtable hold isn’t utilized as a pre-game lobby for the group- a place to show off your skins, mess around and emote, or even prep new relics. Many PvE games have this, and the roundtable hold seems perfect for the task. I also thought it was a missed opportunity that you can’t select your relic loadout during character selection, as what you might want to bring may change depending on the Nightlord you’re facing.

Despite these issues, the Nightlord encounters themselves are genuinely excellent. Each boss feels thoughtfully put together, and I was actually surprised by how much I enjoyed some of the boss themes. The theme for the Equilibrious beast has become one of my all time favorites. It’s also good to see the developers are rolling out (sort of) free content in the form of more beefed up variations of the existing Nightlords.

So on a final note, Nightreign in my opinion succeeds as an experimental departure from the regular Souls formulae, offering a genuinely enjoyable gameplay loop that can create some interesting yet sometimes frustrating moments- depending on the team you end up with, of course. That said, I do wonder if this game could have been a DLC rather than a full standalone release, but either way, it’s a fun game that could really use some more content to lean into the rogue like elements harder. It certainly has potential to be great, and there’s no lack of existing content to draw from in Fromsofts archives. Just keep in mind, this is a drastically different kind of game, so going in with an open mind (and maybe some friends too) is key to experiencing the best that Nightreign has to offer.
